title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Travel Time Estimation in Stochastic Vehicle Routing Problems
abstract: Solving the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) in Stochastic Transportation Networks (STNs), a core task in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), introduces estimation challenges for stochastic path travel times and the resulting VRP objective function. These challenges have typically been addressed through computationally expensive sampling-based techniques such as Monte Carlo simulation, whose performance depends on sample size, the sampling strategy, and the underlying travel time distributions. To address these issues, this study proposes and validates a quantum computing technique, Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) for path-level travel time estimation in STNs. Without relying on sampling or prior assumptions of the travel time distribution, the proposed framework encodes all feasible travel time realizations into a quantum superposition, enabling a theoretical quadratic speed-up over Monte Carlo simulation. Four QAE variants are implemented in IBM's Qiskit framework, namely Canonical AE (CAE), Iterative AE (IAE), Maximum Likelihood AE (MLAE), and Faster AE (FAE), together with four rotation-angle scaling strategies for handling different discrete travel time distributions. Experiments on a small-scale STN show that the choice of scaling method and rotation-angle range significantly affects estimation accuracy, while the four QAE variants produce comparable estimates across all tested conditions, with IAE exhibiting the most stable overall performance. The results provide practical guidance on parameter selection for future hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks in ITS applications.
summary: This paper applies Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) to estimate expected travel times in stochastic vehicle routing problems, offering a theoretical quadratic speed-up over classical Monte Carlo methods. By encoding the entire probability space into a quantum superposition, it provides a powerful tool for hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks in intelligent transportation systems.
main_problem: The core challenge is accurately estimating expected path travel times within Stochastic Vehicle Routing Problems (VRP) in complex transportation networks.
main_result: Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) provides a theoretical quadratic speed-up over classical Monte Carlo simulation for this estimation task, with the Iterative AE variant showing stable performance.
method: The study proposes using QAE to encode all feasible travel time realizations into a quantum superposition state, avoiding sampling and prior distribution assumptions.
model_or_system: The problem is modeled on Stochastic Transportation Networks (STNs) represented as directed graphs with discrete random link travel times. The implementation uses IBM's Qiskit framework.
key_observables: Estimation accuracy, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the performance comparison across four QAE variants (CAE, IAE, MLAE, FAE).
important_parameters: The choice of rotation-angle range ($	ext{[0, 2\pi]}$ vs $	ext{[0, \pi]}$) and scaling method significantly impacts estimation accuracy.
main_assumptions: The work focuses only on the expectation-estimation subproblem; it does not solve the global combinatorial VRP. The results are currently limited by NISQ device noise.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate circuit structures (e.g., 4-qubit toy CAE circuit) and heatmaps showing mean absolute error across various scaling ranges and rotation-angle ranges for different distributions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of classical VRP solving in STNs, then details the QAE methodology to estimate expected travel times, compares four specific QAE variants, and finally analyzes parameter sensitivity (scaling/rotation angle) using experimental results on a small-scale network.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization/transportation, the core technique—using quantum amplitude estimation for expectation value calculation—is a direct application of advanced quantum algorithms relevant to simulating complex physical systems or calculating expectation values in open quantum systems.
